```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# Everything here runs on the hard dependencies and sf's own nc.shp, with three
# exceptions: the maps need ggplot2, the model steps need ranger, and the
# block size from the data needs gstat, all Suggests.  Each gated chunk has a
# note chunk after it that prints when the package is absent, so the article
# builds either way.
has_ggplot <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
has_ranger <- requireNamespace("ranger", quietly = TRUE)
has_gstat  <- requireNamespace("gstat", quietly = TRUE)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo      = TRUE,
  message   = FALSE,
  warning   = FALSE,
  fig.align = "center",
  out.width = "100%"
)
```

spatialkit draws cells from the distribution of the observations, summarises
the observations onto them with standard errors, and scores models on folds
that hold out whole [blocks](glossary.html#block) of the map. The [home page](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/)
says more about why the package exists.

This article is the short path, from installing the package to a map of a
model's predictions, on the North Carolina counties that ship with `sf`.
`vignette("spatialkit_nc_demo")` runs the same steps at length on a simulated
field, and `vignette("glossary")` defines the terms used here.

*This article needs three optional packages: `ggplot2` for the maps, `ranger`
for the model steps and `gstat` for the block size from the data. Where one
is missing, the code that needs it is shown but not run.*

## Installing

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("spatialkit")
```

The development version installs from GitHub:

```{r install-dev, eval=FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("elkronos/gis_modeling_toolkit")
```

Add `build_vignettes = TRUE` to that call to install these articles with it;
building them needs pandoc.

### Optional packages

`sf`, `dplyr`, `logger`, `digest` and `FNN` install with spatialkit. The
packages below are optional; each is needed only for the functions in its row.

| install | for |
|---|---|
| `gstat` | variogram fitting: `estimate_sac_range()`, `make_folds(auto_range = TRUE)`, design effects from a variogram, `kriging_adequacy()` |
| `ranger` | `fit_rf_model()` and `cv_rf()` |
| `sp` | `fit_gwr_model()`, `cv_gwr()`, `gwr_model_selection()` and `compare_models_cv(models = "GWR")` |
| `brms` | `fit_bayesian_spatial_model()` and `cv_bayes()`; it brings `rstan` and `loo` |
| `cmdstanr` | CmdStan as the Stan backend for `brms` (see below) |
| `geometry` | Delaunay triangle tessellations |
| `ggplot2` | every `plot_*()` function and every `plot()` method |
| `patchwork` | the stacked panels in `vignette("spatialkit_nc_demo")` and `example_nc_demo.R` |
| `Matrix` | sparse k-nearest-neighbour weights for Moran's I on large layers |
| `nlme` | REML detrending in `estimate_sac_range()` |
| `tibble` | `make_folds()` returns its `assignment` table as a tibble instead of a data frame |
| `knitr`, `rmarkdown` | building these articles |
| `GWmodel`, `spdep`, `testthat`, `units`, `vctrs`, `withr` | the test suite only |

A call that needs a missing package names it, either in an error that stops
the call or, where the call can go on without the feature, in the log, as
`estimate_sac_range()` does when it returns `NA` without `gstat`.

The Bayesian backend compiles a Stan model for each fit, so it needs a C++
toolchain as well as `brms`. `brms` always brings `rstan`. `cmdstanr` installs
from <https://stan-dev.r-universe.dev>, and `cmdstanr::install_cmdstan()`
builds CmdStan; once a CmdStan build is available,
`fit_bayesian_spatial_model(backend = "auto")` uses it, and otherwise it uses
`rstan`.

## Getting your data in

Data usually arrive as a spatial file or as a table with coordinate columns.
Either way, the next steps need an `sf` layer of POINTs in a projected CRS.

### A spatial file

```{r read-file}
library(sf)
library(spatialkit)

nc <- st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"), quiet = TRUE)
c(features = nrow(nc), geometry = as.character(unique(st_geometry_type(nc))))
```

Those are polygons, and every model here takes points, so reduce them.
`coerce_to_points()` maps a polygon to a point guaranteed to fall inside it,
using `st_point_on_surface()`, a line to its midpoint, and a MULTIPOINT to its
centroid. Attribute columns come along.

```{r to-points}
counties <- ensure_projected(nc[, c("BIR74", "SID74", "NWBIR74")])
obs      <- coerce_to_points(counties)
obs$rate     <- 1000 * obs$SID74 / pmax(obs$BIR74, 1)   # the response
obs$nw_share <- obs$NWBIR74 / pmax(obs$BIR74, 1)        # one predictor

c(points = nrow(obs), geometry = as.character(unique(st_geometry_type(obs))))
```

Every function from here on names the response and the predictors by their
column names, as strings: `response_var = "rate"`,
`predictor_vars = "nw_share"`. `fit_rf_model()` and `fit_gwr_model()` need a
numeric response and stop with an error on a logical, factor or character one;
`cv_rf()` reports that error as the reason every fold failed.
`summarize_by_cell()` warns and leaves such a column out.
`resolution_profile()` takes a numeric or logical response.
`fit_bayesian_spatial_model()` takes a logical or 0/1 response under a family
such as `brms::bernoulli()`, and a factor or character one under
`brms::categorical()` or an ordinal family.

Hex and square grids need a study area. Here it is the union of the counties;
an outline read with `st_read()` serves as well.

```{r boundary}
boundary <- st_as_sf(st_union(counties))
```

### A table with coordinate columns

Here the table is made from the county points so that the example runs. With
your own file, read it with `read.csv()`.

```{r read-table}
ll  <- st_coordinates(st_transform(obs, 4326))
tab <- data.frame(lon = ll[, 1], lat = ll[, 2],
                  births = obs$BIR74, sids = obs$SID74)
head(tab, 2)

pts_ll <- st_as_sf(tab, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)
pts    <- ensure_projected(pts_ll)
```

Pass `crs =` yourself. `st_as_sf()` does not guess it, and the package's
fallback for a layer with no CRS (below) recognises only lon/lat. Lon/lat from
a GPS, a web API or a geocoder is almost always EPSG:4326. A file from a
municipal or national dataset names its CRS in its metadata, and that CRS is
often a projected one.

A table has no polygons to dissolve into a study area. Read an outline if you
have one. Otherwise `clip_target_for()`, called on the points, returns their
bounding box, grown by `expand`, in the projected CRS the points are in or are
moved into. The corners of a box hold no
data, so a hex or square grid over it has cells with no points in them.

The rest of this article carries on with `obs`, the county points.

### Missing values and repeated locations

A row whose response or predictor is `NA`, `NaN` or infinite is dropped
before a fit, with a warning that gives the counts (class
`spatialkit_rows_dropped`). `prep_model_data()` does the dropping, and
`attr(x, "dropped")` says which rows went.

Two observations at the same coordinates are fine for models and folds. A
Voronoi tessellation keeps one seed per location, and every point at that
location is indexed to its cell.

## Coordinates and distance units

Every distance in this package is in the units of the CRS the analysis runs
in. A block size, a GWR bandwidth, a variogram range and a Gaussian process
length-scale are all distances. Give any of them a number in degrees when the
data are in metres and the result is wrong by a factor of about 100,000.
`make_folds()` stops with an error that names the CRS's unit when a block
size would build a grid of more than 1,000,000 blocks.

`ensure_projected()` moves lon/lat data into a projected CRS chosen for their
extent. `nc.shp` arrives in NAD27, a geographic CRS in degrees, and
`ensure_projected()` compared three candidates for the counties, which
`attr(counties, "crs_choice")` holds:

```{r crs}
choice <- attr(counties, "crs_choice")
print(data.frame(name = choice$name,
                 error_percent = round(100 * choice$distance_error, 2),
                 chosen = choice$chosen), row.names = FALSE)
st_crs(counties)$units_gdal
```

It chose a local Albers equal-area projection and logged why:
across this extent the UTM zone distorts distances by
`r with(attr(counties, "crs_choice"), sprintf("%.2f", 100 * distance_error[startsWith(name, "UTM zone")]))`
percent at worst and the Albers projection by
`r with(attr(counties, "crs_choice"), sprintf("%.2f", 100 * distance_error[chosen]))`
percent. Pass `target_crs` to override the choice.

The package writes decisions like this one to the console as `WARN` log
lines, which this article leaves out. `spatialkit_quiet()` turns them off, and
`?"spatialkit-conditions"` says how a log line differs from an R warning.

Areas need an equal-area CRS. For lon/lat data,
`ensure_projected(purpose = "area")` chooses among equal-area projections
only, and `summarize_by_cell(area = TRUE)` stops
with an error when the cells' CRS distorts areas across them by more than 1
percent.

A layer with no CRS at all is read by a documented rule. If the bounding box
fits the lon/lat envelope and the coordinates look like degrees, the layer is
read as EPSG:4326 and projected, with a warning saying so. Set the CRS
yourself if your data are planar and happen to fall in that envelope.

```{r crs-missing, warning=TRUE}
raw <- st_as_sf(data.frame(lon = c(-81.5, -81.1), lat = c(36.4, 36.5)),
                coords = c("lon", "lat"))
st_crs(ensure_projected(raw))$input
```

Two layers that must line up go through `harmonize_crs()`, which returns both in
a common CRS:

```{r harmonize}
pair <- harmonize_crs(obs[1:5, ], st_transform(boundary, 4326))
st_crs(pair$a) == st_crs(pair$b)
```

You do not have to project first. Every function that measures a distance
(`make_folds()`, the `fit_*()` and `cv_*()` functions, `predict_surface()`)
calls `ensure_projected()` on what it is given, so a lon/lat layer is
projected on the way in and the same choice is logged. Calling it yourself,
as above, means the choice is made once and you can see it.

## From points to a map

The calls below take the points to a scored model and a map of its
predictions. The first four draw cells and summarise the observations onto
them; the rest fit a model on the points, score it on folds that hold out
whole blocks, and mark where its predictions apply.

### Cells and their values

```{r pipeline}
# Choose the number of cells.
n_cells <- select_resolution(resolution_profile(obs, "rate"))

# Draw hex cells over the state.
tess <- build_tessellation(obs, boundary = boundary, method = "hex",
                           approx_n_cells = n_cells, quiet = TRUE)

# Put each observation in a cell.
asg <- assign_features_to_polygons(obs, tess$cells)

# Summarise each cell; cells_sf attaches the geometry so the result maps.
cells <- summarize_by_cell(asg, "rate", cells_sf = tess$cells)

c(asked = n_cells$best, drawn = nrow(tess$cells))
```

```{r counts, include=FALSE}
n_drawn <- nrow(tess$cells)
n_empty <- sum(is.na(cells$n))
n_held  <- n_drawn - n_empty
area_km2 <- as.numeric(st_area(cells)) / 1e6
km2 <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",")
and_list <- function(x)
  if (length(x) < 2L) x else paste(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), "and", x[length(x)])
```

`resolution_profile()` sets a size of `r n_cells$obs_per_cell_asked`
observations per cell by default, and `select_resolution()` turns it into a
count of `r n_cells$best` cells. The hex
grid clipped to the state outline has `r n_drawn`. Of these, `r n_empty` hold
no county. They are pieces cut off at the state's edge, of
`r and_list(km2(sort(area_km2[is.na(cells$n)])))` square kilometres, against
`r km2(min(area_km2[!is.na(cells$n)]))` to
`r km2(max(area_km2[!is.na(cells$n)]))` for the cells that hold a county.
`vignette("resolution")` explains the size and the other ways to choose a
count, among them `determine_optimal_levels()`, which reads one off the
clustering of the coordinates.

An observation outside the boundary gets no cell.
`assign_features_to_polygons()` leaves it out, with a warning of class
`spatialkit_unassigned` that gives the count, unless you pass
`keep_unassigned = TRUE`.

```{r summary-cols}
names(cells)
head(st_drop_geometry(cells)[, c("poly_id", "n", "resp_mean_rate",
                                 "..se_resp_rate", "..pooled_resp_rate")], 4)
```

Each row holds the count `n`, the cell's mean `resp_mean_rate` and its
standard error `..se_resp_rate`. A cell with one observation has a standard
error of `NA`, and a cell with none has `n = NA`; both rows are kept, so the
layer has one row per cell. `cell_weight` is the cell's effective sample
size, which equals `n` here, with no design effect and no missing rates; pass
it as the weights of a regression on cell values. `..pooled_resp_rate` is the
[pooled value](glossary.html#pooled-value): the cell's mean pulled toward the mean of the observations in the 8 nearest cells
(nearest by the centroid of their observations), by a weight that grows with
the cell's count. `..pooled_w_resp_rate` holds that weight and
`..pooled_target_resp_rate` the mean it pulls toward. `vignette("cells")`
explains every column, when to widen the standard error with a
[design effect](glossary.html#design-effect) (`deff`), and the warnings `summarize_by_cell()` gives about pooled values.

```{r map-alt, include=FALSE}
mean_range <- range(cells$resp_mean_rate, na.rm = TRUE)
map_alt <- sprintf(paste(
  "North Carolina covered by %d hexagonal cells shaded by their mean SIDS",
  "rate, from %.1f to %.1f per thousand births, with %d small grey",
  "pieces at the state's edge that hold no county."),
  n_held, mean_range[1], mean_range[2], n_empty)
```

```{r map, eval=has_ggplot, fig.height=3.2, fig.alt=map_alt}
plot_tessellation_map(cells, boundary = boundary, fill_col = "resp_mean_rate",
                      legend_title = "mean rate") +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r no-ggplot, echo=FALSE, eval=!has_ggplot, results='asis'}
cat("*(The map needs ggplot2, which is not installed here.)*\n")
```

### Cells or points?

The calls so far give the value of each cell. The model in the next calls is
fitted on the points, which gives it `r nrow(obs)` observations against
`r n_held` cell means. Fit on cells when the
cells are the unit you will report or act on, when the point-level data
cannot leave the building, or when the points are so dense that the cell
means are what the model should see. Either way the folds come from the
points' locations, and the cells can serve as the blocks that define them
(`make_folds(blocks = tess$cells)`).

### A model, scored on held-out blocks

```{r folds}
# Build random folds and folds that hold out whole blocks.
random  <- make_folds(obs, k = 4, method = "random_kfold", seed = 1)
blocked <- make_folds(obs, k = 4, method = "block_kfold", block_size = 100e3,
                      seed = 1)
c(folds = blocked$k, blocks = blocked$params$blocks_used,
  block_width_km = round(blocked$params$block_width / 1e3))
```

```{r county-side, include=FALSE}
county_km <- sqrt(as.numeric(st_area(boundary)) / nrow(obs)) / 1e3
```

`block_size` is a distance in the CRS's units, here metres, and it sets the
smallest edge of a block. The blocks built here are
`r round(blocked$params$block_width / 1e3)` km wide. The wider the blocks, the
farther the held-out points sit from their training data, and the score is
the error at that distance. This article sets 100 km by hand. That is about
`r round(100 / county_km)` counties across (the state's area divided among
its 100 counties gives squares `r round(county_km)` km on a side), and it
gives `r blocked$params$blocks_used` blocks for the four folds.
`vignette("spatial-cross-validation")` is about choosing the size.

`make_folds(auto_range = TRUE)` sizes the blocks from the autocorrelation range
of what the predictors leave unexplained, when `gstat` is installed. A
variogram needs at least thirty points, and below that `estimate_sac_range()`
returns `NA` and says so. On these counties no range is found, and the call
falls back to geometric blocks, with a warning:

```{r auto-range, eval=has_gstat, warning=TRUE}
auto <- make_folds(obs, k = 4, method = "block_kfold", auto_range = TRUE,
                   response_var = "rate", predictor_vars = "nw_share", seed = 1)
```

```{r no-gstat, echo=FALSE, eval=!has_gstat, results='asis'}
cat("*(This step needs gstat, which is not installed here.)*\n")
```

```{r cv, eval=has_ranger}
# Fit and score a random forest on each set of folds.
cv_random  <- cv_rf(obs, "rate", "nw_share", folds = random,
                    num_trees = 300, seed = 1)
cv_blocked <- cv_rf(obs, "rate", "nw_share", folds = blocked,
                    num_trees = 300, seed = 1)
rbind(random  = cv_random$overall[, c("RMSE", "MAE", "R2")],
      blocked = cv_blocked$overall[, c("RMSE", "MAE", "R2")])
```

`cv_rf()` fits a random forest inside every fold and pools the held-out
predictions. The pooled score hides how much the folds disagree, so look at
the range of the per-fold RMSE too:

```{r cv-folds, eval=has_ranger}
rbind(random  = range(cv_random$fold_metrics$RMSE),
      blocked = range(cv_blocked$fold_metrics$RMSE))
```

```{r cv-text, echo=FALSE, eval=has_ranger, results='asis'}
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
ratio <- cv_blocked$overall$RMSE / cv_random$overall$RMSE
rr <- range(cv_random$fold_metrics$RMSE); rb <- range(cv_blocked$fold_metrics$RMSE)
qr <- range(cv_random$fold_metrics$R2);   qb <- range(cv_blocked$fold_metrics$R2)
if (ratio > 1.15) {
  cat("The blocked RMSE is", f2(ratio), "times the random one. The random",
      "folds leave each test point's neighbours in the training set, and the",
      "blocked folds do not.\n\n")
} else {
  cat("The two pooled RMSEs differ by less than the folds do. The random",
      "folds' RMSE runs from", f2(rr[1]), "to", f2(rr[2]), "and the blocked",
      "folds' from", f2(rb[1]), "to", paste0(f2(rb[2]), ".\n\n"))
}
cat("R² is", f2(cv_random$overall$R2), "under random folds and",
    f2(cv_blocked$overall$R2), "under blocked ones. Fold by fold it runs from",
    f2(qr[1]), "to", f2(qr[2]), "under random folds and from", f2(qb[1]), "to",
    paste0(f2(qb[2]), " under blocked ones",
           if (max(qr[1], qb[1]) <= min(qr[2], qb[2]))
             ", so four folds of a hundred counties do not tell the two schemes apart",
           ". R² here is taken about each fold's training mean (`?cv_spatial`),",
           " and on blocks that mean can sit far from the held-out values, so a",
           " blocked R² above 0 does not show that the predictor does better than",
           " the mean of the nearby counties.\n\n"))
cat("The gap between the schemes opens when a model can use its neighbours'",
    "values, through the coordinates or a spatially smooth predictor. The",
    "[quick start on the home page](https://elkronos.github.io/gis_modeling_toolkit/#quick-start)",
    "shows it on a simulated field.\n")
```

```{r cv-none, echo=FALSE, eval=!has_ranger, results='asis'}
cat("*(The model steps need ranger, which is not installed here. With only the",
    "hard dependencies, `cv_spatial()` scores a learner you write with",
    "`new_spatial_fit()`; `vignette(\"models\")` shows how.)*\n")
```

`cv_gwr()` and `cv_bayes()` are the same call for the other two backends, and
`cv_spatial()` takes any learner you write. `compare_models_cv()` runs the
backends on the same folds and puts them in one table.

### A surface, and where it applies

```{r surface, eval=has_ranger}
# Predict on a grid over the state, and mark where the model extrapolates.
fit  <- fit_rf_model(obs, "rate", "nw_share", num_trees = 300, seed = 1)
surf <- predict_surface(fit, n_cells = 4000, covariates = obs,
                        boundary = boundary)
aoa  <- area_of_applicability(surf, model = fit, folds = blocked)
aoa
```

```{r oob-text, echo=FALSE, eval=has_ranger, results='asis'}
oob <- fit$info$oob_r_squared
if (is.finite(oob) && oob < 0.1)
  cat(sprintf(paste(
    "The forest's out-of-bag R², in the print above, is %.2f. Fitted on all",
    "hundred counties, the share of non-white births predicts the SIDS rate",
    "%s better than the mean rate does.\n"),
    oob, if (oob < 0) "no" else "little"))
```

`predict_surface()` returns the grid as points, one per grid node, each
carrying its predictor value from the nearest county. `n_cells = 4000` sets
the grid spacing over the state's bounding box, and `boundary` drops the
nodes outside the state, which leaves
`r if (has_ranger) format(nrow(surf), big.mark = ",") else "fewer"`. The area of
applicability compares each grid point's predictors with the training data.
With `folds = blocked` it sets its threshold from the same folds as the
score.

```{r surface-map, eval=has_ranger && has_ggplot, fig.height=3.2, fig.alt="The random forest's predicted SIDS rate on a fine grid of points over North Carolina, clipped to the state outline, with the hundred county points drawn over it. The surface is low across the west and centre, and highest in one south-central patch and in parts of the east, following the share of non-white births it was fitted on."}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = surf, aes(colour = .pred), size = 1.1) +
  geom_sf(data = boundary, fill = NA, colour = "grey20") +
  geom_sf(data = obs, size = 0.5, colour = "black") +
  scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "predicted rate per thousand births") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r no-ggplot-surface, echo=FALSE, eval=has_ranger && !has_ggplot, results='asis'}
cat("*(The map needs ggplot2, which is not installed here.)*\n")
```

```{r aoa-text, echo=FALSE, eval=has_ranger, results='asis'}
if (aoa$n_inside == aoa$n_new) {
  cat(sprintf(paste(
    "All %s grid points are inside the area of applicability here, because",
    "the grid took its predictor from the nearest county, so no grid point",
    "holds a value the model has not seen.\n"),
    format(aoa$n_new, big.mark = ",")))
} else {
  cat(sprintf("Of the %s grid points, %s are inside the area of applicability.\n",
              format(aoa$n_new, big.mark = ","),
              format(aoa$n_inside, big.mark = ",")))
}
```

When the predictors come from another source, such as a covariate raster
converted to `sf` points and passed as `grid` or `covariates`, this check marks
the parts of the map where the model extrapolates.

## Scripts you can run

Ten numbered scripts, `01` to `10`, install with the package. Each prints what
it is doing and says what to look for before it draws a figure. They use a
simulated field with known structure, so you can check each diagnostic
against the truth.

```{r scripts, eval=FALSE}
dir <- system.file("scripts", package = "spatialkit")
list.files(dir)

source(file.path(dir, "03-folds.R"))    # one topic
source(file.path(dir, "00-run-all.R"))  # all ten, in order
```

| script | topic | needs, beyond `ggplot2` |
|---|---|---|
| `01-tessellations.R` | Voronoi, hex, square and Delaunay cells, and what seeding changes | `geometry` for the Delaunay part |
| `02-resolution.R` | the autocorrelation range, the ladder of counts, the criteria that disagree, choosing the count on half the data, and the default size | `gstat` |
| `03-folds.R` | random against blocked folds, plus buffered leave-one-out and NNDM | `gstat`, to size blocks from the range |
| `04-block-size.R` | sweeping the block size, and the two shapes the curve takes | `gstat`, for the range marker |
| `05-fit-diagnose.R` | wrapping your own model, residual autocorrelation, cell means | `gstat`, for the residual variogram and the kriging check |
| `06-cv-compare.R` | comparing models fold by fold on one set of folds | `ranger`, `sp` or both, for the backend comparison |
| `07-surface-aoa.R` | predicting onto a grid, and the area of applicability | `stars` for the GeoTIFF export; `stars` is not among spatialkit's Suggests |
| `08-feature-select.R` | forward selection, and measuring the selection effect | |
| `09-gwr.R` | GWR coefficients that vary over space | `sp` |
| `10-bayes.R` | a Bayesian GP, and how often its prediction intervals cover the held-out values | `brms` and a Stan toolchain |

The figures need `ggplot2`. When a script lacks a package it skips the part
that needs it, or the whole script for 02, 09 and 10, with a message naming the
package. In an interactive session each script pauses at `[enter]` between
figures; `Sys.setenv(SPATIALKIT_TOUR_PAUSE = "no")` turns the pauses off.
`00-run-all.R` turns them off itself, and most of its running time is script
10, which compiles a Stan model for each fit. Set `SPATIALKIT_TOUR_OUTPUT` to
a folder to write the figures there instead of drawing them.

`example_nc_demo.R` in the same folder is the runnable version of
`vignette("spatialkit_nc_demo")`. It writes its figures to the folder named by
`SPATIALKIT_DEMO_OUTPUT`, or to a temporary folder whose path it prints.

## Next

`vignette("resolution")` comes next: how many cells the data support, and how
to pass that count to the tessellation. The help pages behind this article are
`?ensure_projected`, `?coerce_to_points`, `?resolution_profile`,
`?select_resolution`, `?build_tessellation`, `?assign_features_to_polygons`,
`?summarize_by_cell`, `?make_folds`, `?cv_rf`, `?predict_surface` and
`?area_of_applicability`. `?spatialkit` lists every step of the pipeline with
its functions.
